Who sets and collects property tax

Three county offices do the work, and the state does none of the collecting. The county Director of Equalization values the property, the county Auditor turns the requests of each taxing district into levies, and the county Treasurer collects the bill.

None of the revenue goes to the state, which neither collects nor spends it; the Department of Revenue explains this in its Property Tax 101 sheet. Taxing districts include cities, counties, townships, school districts and special districts such as fire, ambulance, water and road.

Questions about the value on your assessment notice go to the Director of Equalization, while questions about the amount due go to the Treasurer. Having the right office in mind saves a lot of phone tag. If it is about the bill, call the Treasurer. The Department of Revenue keeps contact lists for both on dor.sd.gov.

How a South Dakota home is valued and taxed

A home is assessed at full and true value, which is its market value, as of November 1. The law then equalizes that value to 85 percent to get the taxable value, and the levy is applied to the taxable value.

Assessors combine three approaches for non-agricultural property: cost, market and income. The market and cost approaches are the most common. Agricultural land is valued by a separate productivity formula.

A levy is expressed as dollars per thousand of taxable value. The yearly sequence runs like this: November 1 is the legal assessment date, assessment notices go out March 1, and appeals run from March to June. Taxing district requests are due to the County Auditor October 1, auditors calculate levies by November 1, and the Department of Revenue certifies them. Bills go out and fall due January 1.

A home assessed for the 2021 assessment year is valued as of November 1, 2020, and the taxes are payable in 2022. You pay on a value established the year before.

Owner-occupied classification and the buyer

The owner-occupied classification lowers only the school general fund levy for a primary residence, and it ends when the house is sold. The status continues until the home is sold or its use changes, so the buyer has to apply again.

Other levies, such as county, city and school special education, are the same for every type of property. An owner can be a joint tenant, a life estate owner, a trust beneficiary or a contract for deed buyer, among others, and the dwelling must be the owner's principal residence.

  • Qualifying property: a house, condominium, townhome, manufactured home or a building of four or fewer family units.
  • One per person: an owner can claim the status on only one property statewide.
  • Deadline: file the certificate with the Director of Equalization by March 15 each year.
  • Check your bill: an 'OO' or similar abbreviation on the assessment notice or tax bill shows the status.

If the status is denied, you can appeal. The tests are ownership and occupancy on the November 1 assessment date, that it is the only property you own with the status, that it is your principal residence, and that the certificate was filed by March 15.

Due dates and penalties

January 1 is when the full bill comes due, though paying half by April 30 and the rest by October 31 is allowed. Under SDCL 10-21-23, a first half left unpaid turns delinquent May 1, and a second half November 1.

After a half goes delinquent, each month's first day brings more interest, figured at the Category G rate in SDCL 54-3-16. A bill of fifty dollars or less has to be paid in one payment by April 30. A deadline that lands on a weekend slides to the next working day, and mail postmarked by the last day before delinquency is treated as timely.

Late payment is the costliest mistake on this calendar, because the interest starts the day after a due date and keeps adding up every month. An owner who plans to list in spring should pay the first half on time even if a sale is expected before the second. County offices add their own details, so check with the treasurer in the county you are in.

  • Minnehaha County: taxes turn delinquent May 1 and November 1, with a 10 percent yearly penalty, or .83333 percent a month.
  • Brookings County: partial payments are refused on taxes that are due or delinquent, and paying by card in person adds a 2.5 percent fee.
  • Mead County: delinquent taxpayers cannot pay online, returned payments carry a $40 fee, and a tax certificate sale is held in December.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the local board of equalization. The written appeal is due in mid-March (March 12 in 2026). You must appeal first to the local board or you lose your rights to the later boards; the Department of Revenue's appeal guide walks through each stage.

Two groups skip that step: non-residents, who live outside the local board's jurisdiction, and owners in unorganized townships, who go straight to the county board. Some jurisdictions use a consolidated board, and your assessment notice tells you which applies.

Stage of the appealDeadline or window (2026 schedule)
Assessment notices mailedMarch 1SDCL 10-6-154
Written appeal filed with the local board clerkMarch 12SDCL 10-11-16
Local board meetsMarch 16 to 20SDCL 10-11-13, 10-11-14
Written appeal filed with the county auditorApril 7SDCL 10-11-23
County board meetsApril 14 to May 5SDCL 10-11-25
Appeal filed with the Office of Hearing ExaminersMay 15SDCL 10-11-42
Circuit court, from the county board or OHEWithin 30 days of noticeAppeal guide

The calendar moves each year, so use the guide for the current year. A written appeal can be a letter, an email or a signed PT17 form, and it needs your name, the legal description and a short reason. You also need evidence, such as sales of similar properties. A bare claim that the value is too high will not carry an appeal.

Relief programs and how they affect a sale

A few programs end, or come due, at a sale. The homestead exemption is the one sellers run into most, because it defers taxes instead of removing them.

  • Homestead exemption: delays payment of property taxes until the property is sold. The deferred taxes become a lien and are repaid with interest before any transfer. The age is 70 or older and the deadline is April 1.
  • Assessment freeze: holds the assessed value flat for owner-occupants who are 65 or older or legally disabled. Income limits apply. File by April 1.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: the first $200,000 of valuation is exempt for a veteran rated permanently and totally disabled, with a November 1 deadline. It ends when the property is transferred or sold.
  • Paraplegic veteran exemption: exempts the property from all property taxes until transfer or sale.

Three recent legislative changes also matter. SB 216 (2025) caps annual growth in owner-occupied valuation at 3 percent per county and local budgets at 3 percent, temporarily for five years. SB 245 (2026) uses sales tax revenue to lower school levies. SB 96 (2026) allows a county to levy a local sales tax of up to 0.5 percent and use it to credit owner-occupied property taxes. Call the Property Tax Division at 1-800-829-9188, option 2, to confirm how they apply to your county. Owners planning to sell should ask in particular whether the cap or a new credit changes the bill a buyer will see. Buyers shop on the monthly payment, so a lower tax bill can help your listing.

What happens if taxes go unpaid

On delinquent real estate the county sells a tax certificate, and the holder can later go after a tax deed. Under SDCL 10-25-1, a tax deed proceeding is started after three years from the certificate sale and within six years of it, if the certificate has not been redeemed.

Anyone may redeem a certificate before a deed issues. Under SDCL 10-24-1, the redeeming party pays the treasurer the sum on the certificate, interest at the rate the property sold for, other taxes paid since then and interest on those. The treasurer records the redemption and gives a receipt.

That sequence gives an owner time, but the cost grows. The treasurer can give you the current payoff. Mead County publishes delinquent real estate in public notices before its December sale.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes stay with the property. The Treasurer in the county where it sits can tell you what is owed. If you have a homestead deferral, that lien and its interest must be paid before the title can transfer.

Sellers also owe the state transfer fee of fifty cents per five hundred dollars of value (SDCL 43-4-21). Form PT 56, the Certificate of Real Estate Value, is on the Department of Revenue forms page. Ask the title company whether your deed needs it.

A cash sale leaves these steps as they are. What it drops is the wait on a buyer's loan, which can matter when April 30 or October 31 is near. Any taxes owed are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so get the treasurer's figure before you sign. Before you list, pull your latest tax bill and assessment notice, note whether an owner-occupied or relief status is attached, and write down any open appeal. A buyer's agent will ask about all three, and a clean answer speeds up the title work. If you are behind, a tax certificate sale is the outcome to avoid, so pay or arrange a payoff before the delinquent half drifts toward a certificate sale. We buy South Dakota houses in their current condition, and an offer carries no obligation.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about a high property tax assessment in South Dakota?

Call your county Director of Equalization first. That office can explain how the value was set. If you still disagree, file a written appeal with the local board of equalization by mid-March.

When are South Dakota property taxes due?

The bill is due January 1, with halves payable by April 30 and October 31. An unpaid half is delinquent the next day, May 1 or November 1, and interest then builds each month.

Does the owner-occupied status transfer to the buyer?

No. It continues only until the home is sold or its use changes, so a new owner must apply, with the certificate due by March 15.

Does the owner-occupied status transfer to the buyer?

Yes, through the homestead exemption, for owners 70 or older: the taxes wait until the property is sold. They become a lien with interest, payable before the title can transfer.

How long before a tax certificate becomes a deed?

A tax deed proceeding is initiated after three years from the certificate sale and within six years, under SDCL 10-25-1. Anyone may redeem before a deed issues.

Does a South Dakota house always have to go through probate?

No. South Dakota lets successors collect small estates by affidavit, and the house can pass that way if the decedent's real property interest in the state is $50,000 or less. Larger estates, or any estate where someone needs authority to sell, go through a court-supervised appointment of a personal representative.

The state's probate code is Title 29A of the South Dakota Codified Laws. The clerk of the circuit court is where an application starts.

The affidavit routes are optional shortcuts with strict conditions. Missing one condition, such as a pending application for a personal representative, takes you out of the shortcut.

The two small estate affidavits

One affidavit collects personal property, and the other transfers real property. Each has its own waiting period and dollar limit, and the house falls under the second.

AffidavitWaiting period after deathLimitWhere it comes from
Personal property30 daysEntire estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000SDCL 29A-3-1201
Real property60 daysDecedent's interest in all South Dakota real property does not exceed $50,000SDCL 29A-3-1203

Both affidavits require a statement that no application or petition for a personal representative is pending or has been granted anywhere. Both also require a statement that the decedent owed nothing to the Department of Social Services for medical assistance for nursing home or other institutional care.

For real estate classified as non-agricultural, SDCL 29A-3-1203 lets the value be taken from the assessment rolls for the year of death. Farmland is valued at fair market value on the date of death instead.

How the real property affidavit works

Every person claiming as a successor signs the affidavit. The register of deeds takes the filing, together with a certified or authenticated death certificate, and you file in each county where the decedent held land.

The affidavit has to say who is entitled to the property and on what basis, which can be the homestead allowance, the family allowance, intestate succession or the decedent's will. If the claim is by will, the affiant must state that an investigation found no later will. Each successor's relationship to the decedent and the value of the entire estate go in the affidavit, and everyone signing swears that false statements can bring criminal penalties.

  • Liens and debts stay in place: the successor must apply the property to liens, funeral expenses, administration costs and creditor claims.
  • The successor has the same protection and liability as someone who received a deed of distribution from a personal representative.
  • A secured creditor or judgment creditor keeps its rights against the property.

The statute adds a buyer-protection sentence. A good-faith purchaser or lender who pays value and has no actual notice of a problem takes title free of estate claims, and does not have to investigate whether the transfer was proper. That protection is what lets a buyer close on an affidavit transfer.

Opening a South Dakota probate case

An applicant asks the clerk for informal appointment as personal representative. Under SDCL 29A-3-307, once at least 120 hours have gone by since the death, the clerk, after making the findings required by SDCL 29A-3-308, appoints the applicant, subject to qualification and acceptance.

Informal appointment fully establishes the status, powers and duties of the personal representative. It can be ended under SDCL 29A-3-608 through 29A-3-612, but it cannot be undone backward in time. A nonresident decedent's estate has a 30-day delay unless the domiciliary representative is the applicant or the will directs South Dakota law.

Do not wait. SDCL 29A-3-108 sets a three-year limit after death for starting either kind of probate or appointment, with narrow exceptions.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. SDCL 29A-3-715 spells out a personal representative's powers. They include selling, mortgaging or leasing estate real property for cash, on credit or a mix, unless the will or a court order restricts that.

The same section allows a personal representative to acquire or dispose of land in this or another state at public or private sale. It also allows insurance, repairs, employing attorneys and agents, and paying taxes and administration costs. A will that restricts those powers, or a formal-proceeding order, controls over the default list.

There is a notice rule on sales where the fair market value is not readily ascertainable. At least 14 days before closing, the personal representative must give written notice of the intended sale to persons who have filed a demand for notice under SDCL 29A-3-204. The notice states the property, the purchaser, the price, the payment terms and the security if any payment is deferred.

  • Heirs who want a say in a sale can file a demand for notice.
  • Find out early what proof of authority the title company wants to see.

Debts and creditor claims

Creditors get a limited window. Under SDCL 29A-3-801, the personal representative can run a creditor notice in a county legal newspaper once a week for three weeks in a row. Creditors have four months from the first publication to file or lose the claim.

Known or reasonably ascertainable creditors get written notice by mail or other delivery. Their deadline is four months after the representative's appointment, or 60 days after the notice is sent, whichever is later. A representative need not send notice to a creditor who has already filed a claim, been paid in full, or was neither known nor reasonably ascertainable within four months of appointment.

SDCL 29A-3-803 gives an outer limit for claims arising before death: they are barred unless presented within the time in the published or written notice, or within three years after death. It does not stop proceedings to enforce a mortgage, pledge or other lien on estate property, so a mortgage on the house survives probate. The title company can tell you how it gets paid off at closing.

Closing the estate

An unsupervised estate closes when the personal representative files a verified statement with the court, no sooner than four months after the original appointment. That is SDCL 29A-3-1003.

The statement says the claims period has run or a diligent search for creditors was made, that all inheritance taxes and state estate taxes due have been determined and paid, that the estate has been administered and distributed, and that a copy of the statement and a full accounting went to heirs and devisees and to known creditors whose claims are neither paid nor barred. The accounting can be waived if the people entitled to it consent in writing.

The appointment ends on its own if nothing involving the personal representative is pending a year after the closing statement is filed.

Transfer fees on an inherited house

Under SDCL 43-4-21 the grantor pays a state transfer fee of fifty cents on every five hundred dollars of value. That applies to a normal sale from a personal representative or from successors to a buyer.

SDCL 43-4-22 exempts some estate transfers, such as those made under a decree of distribution and those between a fiduciary and a beneficiary to serve the fiduciary relationship. A sale to a buyer for money is a different transaction, so expect the fee on a sale unless your title company says otherwise.

Taxes on the house still follow the normal county calendar. Property taxes on the house run on the county calendar: due January 1, payable in two halves by April 30 and October 31.

When a cash sale makes sense for an heir

A cash sale can help when an heir lives out of state, when the house needs repairs, or when carrying costs are mounting while the estate is open. It spares the estate repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval. It does not shortcut the probate steps above, because someone with authority still has to sign the deed. Heirs often ask what the order of events looks like. Someone files with the clerk, the clerk appoints a personal representative, and that person publishes the creditor notice and collects what the estate owns. Only then does a deed to a buyer make sense, unless the small estate affidavit fits. If an heir is hundreds of miles away, the personal representative can still handle signing, so the heir does not need to travel for every step. For a first conversation with a buyer or title company, gather the death certificate, the will if there is one, any letters of appointment or recorded affidavit, and the latest tax bill.

Frequently asked questions

How long do I have to open probate in South Dakota?

About three years from the date of death, under SDCL 29A-3-108. A few exceptions exist, but waiting limits what a personal representative can do.

Can I sell inherited property in South Dakota without probate?

Sometimes. If the decedent's South Dakota real property interest is $50,000 or less, successors may use the real property affidavit 60 days after death, and a good-faith purchaser takes title free of estate claims. Otherwise a personal representative usually signs the deed.

How long do creditors have to file claims against an estate?

Four months from first publication when a notice runs. Known creditors who get written notice have four months from appointment or 60 days from the notice, whichever is later. All claims are barred three years after death.

Does a mortgage disappear when the owner dies?

No. The claims deadlines in SDCL 29A-3-803 do not block enforcement of a mortgage or other lien on estate property.

Who pays the South Dakota transfer fee on a sale?

The seller, at fifty cents per five hundred dollars of value (SDCL 43-4-21). Transfers under a decree of distribution in an estate are exempt.
